newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy employers' chief says pessimism must not win.
newsitem.headline: Italy employers' chief says pessimism must not win.

text.p: The head of the Italian employers' federation urged businessmen on Sunday to fight the economic slowdown and not give into pessimism.
In an open letter to members of the Confindustria organisation, Giorgio Fossa said 1996 had been a "grey year" and added that Italy's centre-left government had done nothing to make things better.
"But we need to roll up our sleeves and overcome our resignation," Fossa said in his letter.
"We have to continue to compete in a world which every day is changing and becoming more difficult," he added.
But in order to compete, companies would have to reduce their labour costs, Fossa said in an apparent reference to the long-running dispute in the metalworkers and engineering sector.

Talks between unions and management over the renewal of contracts in the sector, which accounts for some 40 percent of manufacturing output in Italy, have dragged on for months, with the two sides further apart than ever.
Labour Minister Tiziano Treu has called a meeting of unions and employers next week in a bid to end the deadlock.

Fossa has launched several stinging attacks against Prime Minister Romano Prodi in recent weeks and in his end of year message, he again criticised the seven-month-old government for failing to support industry.

He said economic growth was being hampered by an increasingly heavy tax burden being placed on businesses, by the sluggish privatisation programme and by the failure of the government to introduce more flexible working practices.

Fossa said employers supported Prodi's drive to book Italy a place among the founder nations of the planned single European currency, but said he was going about it the wrong way, raising taxes instead of cutting back on state spending.

Industrialists have been especially critical of the 1997 budget, which aims to take 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) off next year's projected budget deficit. The package relies heavily on revenue raising measures including a contested "Euro Tax". $1 = 1,529 lire
